data.sourcePassage:
A linear search, sometimes called a sequential search, is one of the simplest ways a computer can locate a value in a list. The algorithm begins at the very first item and compares it to the target value it is looking for. If the two values match, the search is complete and the position of the item is returned. If they do not match, the algorithm moves on to the next item and repeats the comparison. This process continues, one item at a time, until either the target is found or every item in the list has been checked without success.

Because a linear search checks items one by one, the number of comparisons it makes depends entirely on where the target happens to sit in the list. In the best case, the target is the very first item, so only a single comparison is needed. In the worst case, the target is the last item in the list, or it is not present at all — in either situation, every single item must be checked. For a list of one hundred items, this could mean up to one hundred comparisons.

One of the most important advantages of a linear search is that it works on any list, regardless of whether the items are sorted into any particular order. This makes it very flexible. If a list is small — say, fewer than twenty items — a linear search is often perfectly adequate and is simple enough to write quickly in code.

However, for very large lists, a linear search becomes inefficient. Imagine searching through a list of one million names: in the worst case, the algorithm would need to make one million comparisons. Because the number of comparisons grows in direct proportion to the size of the list, computer scientists say a linear search is slow for large datasets. In such situations, a different algorithm — such as binary search — is usually a better choice, provided the list is sorted.

data.sourcePassage:
Binary search is a much more efficient searching algorithm than linear search, but it comes with one strict requirement: the list must be sorted before the search can begin. If the list is not in order, binary search will produce incorrect results and cannot be relied upon.

The algorithm works by finding the middle element of the list and comparing it to the target value. If the middle element matches the target, the search is over. If the target is smaller than the middle element, the algorithm discards the right half of the list entirely — it knows the target cannot be in that half — and repeats the process on the left half. If the target is larger than the middle element, the left half is discarded and the search continues in the right half. Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining items, which is why binary search is so powerful.

Consider searching for the number 14 in the sorted list [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20]. The middle element is 11. Since 14 is greater than 11, the left half is discarded. The new search space is [14, 17, 20]. The middle element is now 17. Since 14 is less than 17, the right portion is discarded, leaving just [14]. That single element matches the target — found in just three comparisons.

To appreciate why this efficiency matters, consider a sorted list of 1,000 items. A linear search might need up to 1,000 comparisons to find the target. Binary search, by contrast, needs at most around 10 comparisons, because each step halves the remaining search space. For a list of one million items, binary search would need at most about 20 comparisons. This dramatic difference means binary search is the preferred choice whenever working with large, sorted datasets.

data.sourcePassage:
Bubble sort is a sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly comparing adjacent pairs of elements in a list and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. The algorithm performs multiple passes through the list, each pass moving the next-largest unsorted element into its correct position at the end of the list. With each completed pass, one more element is settled in place, and the unsorted portion of the list shrinks by one.

To see how this works, consider the list [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]. During the first pass, the algorithm compares 5 and 3 — they are in the wrong order, so they are swapped to give [3, 5, 8, 1, 4]. Next, 5 and 8 are compared — they are already in order, so no swap occurs. Then 8 and 1 are compared — they are in the wrong order, so they are swapped: [3, 5, 1, 8, 4]. Finally, 8 and 4 are compared and swapped: [3, 5, 1, 4, 8]. After this first pass, 8 has 'bubbled up' to its correct final position at the end.

The name 'bubble sort' comes from this behaviour: the largest unsorted value gradually bubbles its way to the top (or end) of the list over each pass, just as air bubbles rise to the surface of water. After each pass, the largest remaining unsorted element is guaranteed to be in the correct position, so the next pass can ignore the last element and focus on a slightly shorter portion of the list.

For a list of n items, bubble sort may need up to n minus one passes in the worst case to fully sort the list. This makes bubble sort quite slow for large lists, as the number of comparisons grows rapidly with list size. However, bubble sort is straightforward to understand and to trace by hand, which is why it is often used as a teaching tool when first introducing sorting algorithms.
